name: Venlafaxine (Effexor XR)
summary: SNRI antidepressant used for depression and several anxiety disorders. Often starts helping in 1–2 weeks, with fuller benefits by 4–6 weeks. Can raise blood pressure at higher doses and is known for a rough withdrawal if stopped too fast.
description: Venlafaxine (Effexor XR) is an antidepressant that also treats anxiety. It’s not a “take it and feel it in an hour” med—most people notice early shifts in 1–2 weeks, with bigger changes by 4–6 weeks. Common side effects include nausea, sweating, insomnia or sleepiness, and sexual side effects. The biggest “respect this med” issues are: (1) suicidal thoughts risk in younger people early in treatment, (2) dose-related blood pressure increases, (3) serotonin syndrome with certain drug combos, and (4) discontinuation symptoms if you miss doses or stop abruptly.
patient_summary: Venlafaxine can treat depression and anxiety, but it takes time—usually 1–2 weeks for early signs and 4–6 weeks for real traction. Side effects often show up before benefits (nausea, sweating, sleep changes, sexual side effects). The two big rules: monitor mood closely early on (especially under 25), and don’t stop suddenly—this one is famous for withdrawal symptoms.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for unipolar major depression. Early improvement may show up in 1–2 weeks, with fuller response often 4–6 weeks (and sometimes longer depending on severity).
FDA-approved for generalized anxiety disorder. Many people notice early changes within ~2 weeks, but meaningful improvement often continues through weeks 4–6.
FDA-approved for panic disorder (with or without agoraphobia) using the extended-release capsule formulation. Start low and titrate slowly to reduce activation and jitteriness early on.
FDA-approved for social anxiety disorder. Some clinicians hold the initial therapeutic dose for several weeks before pushing higher, because benefit often builds over time.
Used off-label for PTSD in adults. Doses in trials often land around the mid-range, and some patients need higher doses for a full trial.
Sometimes used as an alternative when SSRIs don’t deliver enough benefit. Higher doses may be used, but the side effect and blood pressure profile matters.
An alternative option for PMDD, typically with gradual dose changes over cycles, not rapid day-to-day adjustments.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to venlafaxine or any component of the formulation
Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Starting an MAOI within 7 days of stopping venlafaxine (many experts prefer a longer washout)
Initiation in patients receiving IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.patient_text: Venlafaxine is a “build over time” medication. Many people notice early shifts (slightly less dread, fewer spirals, a bit more function) within 1–2 weeks, but the bigger, steadier improvement usually shows up over 4–6 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption is high; extended-release absorbs more slowly than immediate-release
pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: early effects often 1–2 weeks; anxiety disorders: early effects may appear within ~2 weeks; continued improvement commonly 4–6 weeks (sometimes longer for OCD/PTSD)
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate-release: venlafaxine ~2 hours, ODV ~3 hours; extended-release formulations peak later
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Venlafaxine: ~5 hours (IR), ~10.7 hours (ER hydrochloride); ODV: ~11–12.5 hours
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Requires divided dosing (2–3 times/day) at higher totals
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via CYP2D6 to active metabolite O-desmethylvenlafaxine (ODV)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily urine (~87%) as metabolites and a small amount unchanged
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Recommended with food to improve tolerability; XR is taken once daily at about the same time

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Venlafaxine (Effexor XR) is an SNRI antidepressant that treats depression and several anxiety disorders. It’s not a quick sedative—this is a daily medication that builds over weeks. In psychiatry, it’s commonly used when anxiety and depression are both in the picture, or when an SSRI wasn’t enough.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, low energy, impaired function
{link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)}: Excessive worry, tension, and mental “stuckness” that doesn’t shut off
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic Disorder}: Recurrent panic attacks and fear of more attacks
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder}: Intense fear of judgment, avoidance, performance anxiety that impacts life
off_label: {link:condition:obsessive-compulsive-disorder:OCD} as an alternative when SSRIs aren’t enough
PMDD as an alternative option (not first-line)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Real talk: with venlafaxine, side effects can show up before the benefits. Most people don’t feel “different” on day one. They notice change because their days start going a little smoother over time.

quotes: The nausea was loud at first, then it chilled out.
I felt a little wired and sleepy at the same time.
My anxiety spiked for a few days and then leveled off.
items.note: Early activation (jittery, restless, more anxious) can happen. Starting low and going up gradually helps.

quotes: It wasn’t a magic switch. It was more like… fewer bad days in a row.
My spirals got shorter. I still had anxiety, but it didn’t hijack my whole day.
I started doing things again without having to white-knuckle it.
items.note: Most meaningful gains often build between weeks 4–6 (sometimes longer in tougher cases).

quotes: I couldn’t fall asleep for a bit, so we moved it to morning and that helped.
I felt sleepy during the day at first.
items.note: Venlafaxine can push sleep either direction: insomnia or sleepiness. Timing and dose changes can matter.

quotes: My libido dipped and orgasms took forever.
Everything worked, but it felt… muted.
It helped my anxiety, but sex got complicated.
items.note: This is common with serotonergic meds. If it’s a dealbreaker, there are workarounds.

quotes: If I missed one dose, I felt weird within a day—dizzy and zappy.
Stopping fast was brutal. Never again.
The brain zaps were the worst. Tapering slowly saved me.
items.note: Venlafaxine has a reputation for discontinuation symptoms. Consistency and slow tapers matter.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Venlafaxine is a daily med that builds. You usually don’t feel it like a sedative. You notice it because your baseline starts to shift.
key_points: Days 1–7: Side effects may show up first (nausea, sweating, sleep changes, jittery energy)
Weeks 1–2: Early signs can appear (slightly less intensity, a bit more function)
Weeks 4–6: Where a lot of people get their real traction
Up to 12 weeks: Some anxiety conditions (especially OCD/PTSD patterns) may need a longer trial
Missing doses: Discontinuation symptoms can start within 24–48 hours in some people

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Venlafaxine is effective for depression and several anxiety disorders, but the key is giving it enough time at a dose your body can tolerate. A common pattern is: side effects early, then gradual improvements in mood, anxiety “volume,” and day-to-day functioning over the next month or two. If someone isn’t moving at all after a full trial (usually 6+ weeks at a therapeutic dose), that’s when clinicians consider dose optimization, augmentation, or switching.
sections.clinical_details: In practice, clinicians often hold a therapeutic dose for several weeks before increasing, because response can keep improving without chasing higher doses too quickly. For panic disorder, some experts keep 75 mg for ~6 weeks before pushing higher. For depression, dose increases may be spaced out (eg, every 4 to 6 weeks) when things aren’t urgent and tolerability is the limiting factor.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If you’re under 25, mood can worsen early on. This is why we monitor closely—especially in the first 1–2 months or when doses change.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Venlafaxine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Do not combine with MAOIs. Serious reactions (including serotonin syndrome) can occur. A washout period is required when switching.
Blood pressure can rise in a dose-related way. Higher doses = higher risk. People with baseline hypertension need extra caution.
Activation of mania/hypomania can occur, especially if someone has bipolar vulnerability. Screen for bipolar disorder before starting.
Serotonin syndrome risk increases when combined with other serotonergic medications or certain interacting drugs.
Stopping abruptly (or missing multiple doses) can cause significant withdrawal symptoms.
patient_counseling: If you’re under 25 (or have a history of suicidal thoughts), tell your prescriber ASAP if mood gets darker, agitation ramps up, or you feel suddenly impulsive.
Take it consistently. Missing doses can make you feel awful fast (dizziness, “brain zaps,” irritability).
If your blood pressure runs high, you’ll want regular BP checks—especially during titration.
Call immediately for symptoms that look like serotonin syndrome: confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea, agitation, fast heart rate.
If you notice new manic symptoms (not sleeping, racing thoughts, grandiosity, risky behavior), don’t ignore it—get assessed.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: nausea, sweating, dry mouth, insomnia or sleepiness, dizziness, nervousness, and sexual side effects. Venlafaxine can also raise blood pressure, especially at higher doses, and is known for discontinuation symptoms if stopped too fast.
plain_language_list: Insomnia or sleepiness (it can go either way)
Sexual side effects (lower libido, delayed orgasm, erectile issues)
Withdrawal symptoms if doses are missed or stopped abruptly (dizziness, “brain zaps,” irritability, insomnia)

common.patient_note: This is one of the most common early side effects. Taking it with food and starting low can help. For many people it fades as the body adjusts.
If it revs you up, morning dosing may help. If it makes you sleepy, evening may make more sense. Timing is a legit tool.
Some people feel sedated or foggy early on. Be careful with driving until you know your reaction.
Often worse with missed doses or rapid dose changes. Hydration and slower titration can help.
Can be annoying and persistent for some people. If it’s intense, it’s worth discussing dose and alternatives.
This can look like lower desire, delayed orgasm, anorgasmia, or erectile issues. If it’s impacting quality of life, there are strategies—don’t just suffer in silence.

serious: Suicidal thoughts/behavior risk in people 18–24 early in treatment or during dose changes: requires close monitoring.
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea, fast heart rate—medical emergency if severe.
Clinically significant blood pressure elevation or hypertensive crisis (rare, more likely at higher doses).
Mania/hypomania activation: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior—needs urgent reassessment for bipolar spectrum.
Hyponatremia/SIADH (especially older adults): confusion, weakness, headache, falls; can be severe.
Bleeding risk (especially with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, anticoagulants): easy bruising, GI bleed symptoms.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma (rare): eye pain, vision changes, redness—emergency.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Venlafaxine plays in the serotonin and norepinephrine space, so the biggest interaction risks are serotonin syndrome, bleeding risk, and washout rules with MAOIs.

items.with: MAOIs (and other strong MAOI-like agents, including certain antibiotics in this category)
items.risk: High risk of serious reactions, including serotonin syndrome. Contraindicated.
items.action: Do not combine. Allow at least 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting venlafaxine. When stopping venlafaxine before an MAOI, the manufacturer recommends 7 days, though many experts use a longer washout.

items.with: Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, linezolid, certain opioids, St. John’s wort, lithium, etc.)
items.risk: Increased serotonin syndrome risk (usually when multiple serotonergic agents are combined).
items.action: Use caution and educate on symptoms. Avoid unnecessary stacking. Seek medical care for severe symptoms.

items.risk: Increased bleeding risk (bruising, GI bleeding, postpartum hemorrhage risk late in pregnancy).
items.action: Use the lowest effective doses, monitor for bleeding, and reassess if easy bruising or GI symptoms appear.

items.risk: Worsened impairment, dizziness, sedation, and judgment problems (even though venlafaxine isn’t primarily a sedative).
items.action: Limit or avoid alcohol, especially early in treatment or during dose changes.

items.with: Medications that raise blood pressure or heart rate (stimulants, certain decongestants)
items.risk: Additive increases in BP/HR, especially at higher venlafaxine doses.
items.action: Monitor BP/HR more closely. Adjust plan if BP climbs.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Venlafaxine is one of the classic “don’t stop me suddenly” antidepressants. If you quit abruptly (or even miss a couple doses), you can get a discontinuation syndrome that feels like dizziness, nausea, brain zaps, irritability, anxiety, and insomnia. The move is a slow, planned taper—especially after higher doses or longer treatment.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks, a common approach is tapering over ~2–4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to catch returning symptoms early.
Shorter treatment (2–3 weeks) may be tapered over 1–2 weeks; <2 weeks often doesn’t require a taper, but sensitivity varies.
Reasons to taper slower (≥4 weeks or longer): history of withdrawal symptoms, higher doses, long-term use (>6 months), or prior severe discontinuation syndrome.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: go back to the previous tolerated dose and taper more gradually from there.
Because venlafaxine has a relatively short half-life, discontinuation symptoms can appear within 24–48 hours in some people.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Venlafaxine comes in immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (XR/ER). In psychiatry, XR is commonly preferred because it’s once-daily and tends to be smoother. Start low, titrate gradually, and give each dose level enough time to work before chasing higher numbers—unless symptoms are severe and urgent.

adult.mdd_xr_initial: 37.5 to 75 mg PO once daily (XR/ER). If starting at 37.5 mg, increase to 75 mg once daily after 4 to 7 days as tolerated.
adult.mdd_xr_titration: Increase by ≤75 mg/day increments at intervals of ≥4 days based on response and tolerability (often slower, every 4 to 6 weeks, when clinically appropriate).
adult.mdd_xr_max: 225 mg/day per manufacturer labeling (some guidelines and specialist practice may go higher with limited experience).
adult.mdd_ir_initial: 37.5 to 75 mg/day PO; doses >37.5 mg/day are given in 2 to 3 divided doses.
adult.mdd_ir_titration: Increase by ≤75 mg/day at intervals of ≥4 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.gad_xr_initial: 37.5 to 75 mg PO once daily (XR/ER). If starting at 37.5 mg, increase to 75 mg once daily after 4 to 7 days as tolerated.
adult.gad_xr_titration: Increase by ≤75 mg/day increments at intervals of ≥4 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.panic_xr_initial: 37.5 mg PO once daily for 1 week, then increase to 75 mg once daily after 7 days as tolerated.
adult.panic_xr_titration: Increase by ≤75 mg/day increments at intervals of ≥7 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.social_anxiety_xr_initial: 37.5 mg PO once daily; after 3 to 7 days, increase to 75 mg/day.
adult.social_anxiety_xr_titration: Maintain 75 mg/day for 4 to 7 weeks, then increase by 37.5 mg increments weekly based on response and tolerability.
adult.ptsd_xr_titration: Increase by ≤75 mg/day increments at intervals of ≥4 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.ptsd_xr_typical: Average doses in trials around ~170 mg/day (varies).
adult.ptsd_xr_max: Up to 300 mg PO once daily has been used in some protocols (off-label).
adult.ocd_initial: 75 mg/day (XR once daily or IR in 3 divided doses) as an alternative option when SSRIs are insufficient (off-label).
adult.ocd_titration: Increase by 75 mg every 2 weeks to 225 mg/day; may increase further based on response and tolerability.
adult.ocd_max: Up to 350 mg/day has been used in some expert recommendations (off-label).
adult.renal_impairment: CrCl ≥30 mL/min: no adjustment typically needed. CrCl <30 mL/min (or dialysis): start 37.5 mg once daily; titrate cautiously; do not exceed 50% of the usual maximum recommended dose.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A to C): start 37.5 mg/day; increase by ≤37.5 mg/day at intervals ≥1 week. Do not exceed 50% of the usual recommended dose or 150 mg/day (whichever is less) for ER hydrochloride; use with caution. ER besylate should not be used to initiate or taper due to limited lower strengths.
adult.older_adults: Refer to adult dosing; use with caution. Older adults have higher risk of hyponatremia/SIADH and falls—start low, titrate slowly, monitor sodium and BP.

sections.simple_explanation: XR/ER is usually once daily and smoother. IR is split into 2–3 doses when totals are higher. The goal is the lowest effective dose that improves symptoms without pushing side effects (especially blood pressure).

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Venlafaxine can be used in pregnancy and breastfeeding when clinically indicated, but it’s usually not the first-line “starter” option for someone treatment-naïve. Decisions should be individualized and shared—balancing untreated illness risks against medication exposure risks. For older adults, the big watch-outs are hyponatremia (SIADH), falls, and blood pressure.
sections.pregnancy: Venlafaxine and its active metabolite cross the placenta. SNRI exposure late in pregnancy can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (often resolves within ~2 weeks) and, rarely, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Stopping or dose-reducing right before delivery to prevent neonatal symptoms is not generally recommended. Untreated depression and anxiety also carry real pregnancy risks, so the plan should be individualized using shared decision-making and the lowest effective single-agent dose when possible.
sections.lactation: Venlafaxine and ODV are present in breast milk. Reported relative infant dose (RID) often falls in the ~6% to 9% range in pooled or observational data, with variability. Many infants in case series had no reported adverse effects, but infants should be monitored for sedation and adequate weight gain. If starting an antidepressant for the first time postpartum in a breastfeeding, treatment-naïve patient, other agents may be preferred; venlafaxine can be considered with caution when clinically appropriate.
sections.pediatrics: Venlafaxine is not approved for use in pediatric patients. Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. If used off-label in adolescents (eg, treatment-resistant depression), dosing is specialized and requires very close monitoring for suicidality, activation, and other adverse effects.
sections.geriatrics: Use with caution in adults ≥65. Beers Criteria flags SNRIs (including venlafaxine) for risk of SIADH/hyponatremia—monitor sodium, especially after starting or dose changes. Also use caution in patients with severe hypertension or recurrent falls.
sections.hepatic: Clearance is reduced in cirrhosis. Start low (often 37.5 mg/day) and titrate slowly (≤37.5 mg increments at ≥1 week intervals), with dose caps based on severity and clinical response.
sections.renal: In significant renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min or dialysis), start 37.5 mg/day and titrate cautiously, generally limiting to ≤50% of usual maximum dosing due to reduced clearance and higher variability.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and clinical worsening: especially ages 18–24 and during the first 1–2 months or during dose changes. Monitor for new/worsening depression, agitation, impulsivity, insomnia, and unusual behavior changes.
Blood pressure and heart rate: check regularly, especially at higher doses and in patients with preexisting hypertension. Venlafaxine can cause dose-related BP increases and modest HR increases.
Bipolar screening: assess personal/family history of bipolar disorder, mania, hypomania prior to starting; monitor for mood switching.
Discontinuation symptoms: ask about missed doses and withdrawal symptoms; plan tapers proactively.
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk (especially older adults): consider baseline sodium in high-risk patients and recheck after initiation or dose increases.
Bleeding risk: monitor for bruising or GI bleeding symptoms if combined with NSAIDs/antiplatelets/anticoagulants.
Ocular symptoms: monitor for acute angle-closure glaucoma warning signs in at-risk patients (eye pain, redness, sudden vision changes).
Weight and appetite changes: venlafaxine can cause weight loss in some patients; monitor if clinically relevant.
Lipids: periodic lipid panel may be reasonable in long-term treatment or if hypercholesterolemia emerges.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Venlafaxine comes as immediate-release tablets and extended-release capsules/tablets. In most psychiatric use, XR/ER is preferred because it’s once daily and tends to be more tolerable for many people.
items: Extended-release capsule (hydrochloride): 37.5 mg, 75 mg, 150 mg (e.g., Effexor XR and generics)
Immediate-release tablet (hydrochloride): 25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg (generics)
Extended-release tablet 24-hour (hydrochloride): 37.5 mg, 75 mg, 150 mg, 225 mg (generics)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Venlafaxine (and its active metabolite, ODV) blocks the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, which increases signaling in brain circuits involved in mood and anxiety. At lower doses, it acts more “SSRI-like” (mostly serotonin). As the dose increases, norepinephrine effects become more noticeable—this is part of why blood pressure can rise at higher doses.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Venlafaxine is a strong option when depression and anxiety overlap, when symptoms are more severe, or when an SSRI didn’t quite get someone there. It’s also used for panic and social anxiety in XR form. Clinically, the main trade-offs are tolerability (especially nausea/activation early), blood pressure monitoring at higher doses, and the reality that it can be tough to stop if tapered too quickly.

seo.title: Venlafaxine (Effexor XR): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Withdrawal
seo.description: Effexor XR (venlafaxine) for depression and anxiety: dosing (37.5–225 mg+), how long it takes to work, common side effects (nausea, sweating, sexual effects), blood pressure monitoring, serotonin syndrome risk, and how to taper safely to avoid withdrawal.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is venlafaxine (Effexor XR) used for?
faqs.a: Venlafaxine is used for major depression and several anxiety disorders, including generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), panic disorder, and social anxiety disorder. It’s a daily medication that builds over weeks—not an immediate calm-down pill.

faqs.q: How long does Effexor XR take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes in 1–2 weeks (less intensity, fewer spirals), but the bigger improvement typically builds over 4–6 weeks. Some anxiety patterns can take longer for a full trial.

faqs.q: Why do people say Effexor withdrawal is intense?
faqs.a: Because venlafaxine has a relatively short half-life, and discontinuation symptoms can show up fast—sometimes within 24–48 hours—especially if doses are missed or stopped abruptly. Symptoms can include dizziness, nausea, irritability, insomnia, and “brain zaps.” Slow tapering helps a lot.

Yes. Blood pressure increases are dose-related—more likely at higher doses. Most increases are modest, but clinically significant hypertension can happen. If you have baseline high blood pressure, you’ll want regular BP checks, especially during dose increases.

faqs.q: Is there a suicidality warning with venlafaxine?
faqs.a: Yes. Like other antidepressants, venlafaxine carries a warning that short-term studies showed increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients. This is why close monitoring is emphasized in the first 1–2 months and during dose changes—especially for people under 25.

It can. Antidepressants can precipitate mania or hypomania, especially if someone has bipolar vulnerability. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar disorder and watch for signs like decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior, and unusually elevated mood.

faqs.q: What are the most common Effexor XR side effects?
faqs.a: Common side effects include nausea, sweating, dry mouth, dizziness, insomnia or sleepiness, nervousness early on, and sexual side effects (lower libido, delayed orgasm, erectile issues). Many early side effects improve as your body adjusts.

faqs.q: Can I take Effexor XR with other antidepressants or triptans?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it depends. Combining multiple serotonergic medications can increase serotonin syndrome risk. Your prescriber weighs benefits vs risk and will tell you what symptoms to watch for (agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, muscle rigidity).

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Effexor XR and immediate-release venlafaxine?
faqs.a: Effexor XR is extended-release and usually taken once daily with smoother blood levels. Immediate-release venlafaxine is typically taken 2–3 times per day at higher totals. XR is often preferred in psychiatry for convenience and tolerability.

faqs.q: Is venlafaxine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It can be used when clinically indicated, but it’s often not the first-choice starter medication for treatment-naïve patients. Decisions should be individualized. Late-pregnancy exposure may be linked to neonatal adaptation symptoms, and venlafaxine/ODV are present in breast milk—so infants are monitored for sedation and weight gain.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it’s close to the next dose—then skip and resume your schedule. Don’t double up without medical advice. If missed doses trigger dizziness or brain zaps, tell your prescriber; timing and taper strategy may need adjusting.
